title: How can i get SQL Injection

preconditions: User input is concatenated into a SQL query without parameterization
An input point that reaches a database query is reachable pre- or post-auth

process.action: Identify parameters that influence database-backed responses (search, filters, sort, IDs)
process.expected_observation: Parameter values affect returned data set

process.action: Send syntax-breaking probes (single quote, boolean true/false pairs) and diff responses
process.expected_observation: Error message, status code, or content length differs between true/false conditions

process.action: Confirm injection class (error-based, boolean-blind, time-based blind, UNION-based)
process.expected_observation: Consistent, controllable behavior change tied to injected logic

process.action: Enumerate database metadata (version, current user, schema) via the confirmed technique
process.expected_observation: Database name/version/table names extracted

process.action: Extract sensitive table contents or attempt privilege escalation (e.g. UNION into admin tables, stacked queries)
process.expected_observation: Sensitive data retrieved, confirming full impact

impact: Full database read/write, including credentials and PII
Authentication bypass via crafted login queries
In some configurations, OS command execution via database features (e.g. xp_cmdshell)
remediation: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements exclusively; never concatenate user input into SQL
Apply least-privilege database accounts per application function
Add a WAF as defense-in-depth, not as the primary control

preconditions: User-controlled input (query params, form fields, headers) is reflected in the HTML response
No or insufficient output encoding/CSP is applied to the reflected context

process.action: Identify all input points that are echoed back in the response
process.expected_observation: Input value appears unmodified in the HTML/JS/attribute context

process.expected_observation: Context dictates which payload shape will execute

process.action: Send a canary payload to confirm reflection without encoding
process.expected_observation: Special characters like < > " ' pass through unescaped

process.action: Craft a context-appropriate payload that breaks out and executes JavaScript
process.expected_observation: JavaScript executes in the victim's browser origin (e.g. alert/document.cookie access)

title: Saving more than 100,000 website from a Watering Hole attack

scenario.summary: Web Cache Poisoning writeup against HubSpot.
preconditions: A shared cache stores responses keyed on a subset of the request that excludes an input the origin server's response actually varies on (an 'unkeyed input')

process.action: Identify cacheable responses and the cache key components (via cache-control/age headers and response timing)
process.expected_observation: Response is confirmed cacheable and shared across requests

process.action: Discover unkeyed inputs (headers/params that affect the response but are not part of the cache key)
process.expected_observation: A header (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) changes the response content without changing the cache key

process.action: Inject a malicious value into the unkeyed input (e.g. attacker domain into X-Forwarded-Host used to build a resource URL) and trigger caching of the poisoned response
process.expected_observation: Poisoned response is cached with attacker-controlled content

process.action: Verify a subsequent unauthenticated request retrieves the poisoned, cached response
process.expected_observation: Victim requests receive the attacker-controlled content directly from cache

impact: Mass client-side attack (XSS/malicious redirect) served to every visitor via the shared cache
Denial of service by poisoning the cache with error responses
remediation: Ensure the cache key includes every input that affects the response, or strip/normalize unkeyed inputs at the edge
Validate and canonicalize headers like Host/X-Forwarded-Host before using them to construct responses
Use short cache TTLs and cache-busting validation for sensitive/dynamic content

title: mfa bypass in private program, the abdulsec way

preconditions: A login flow has a distinct second-factor step that can be skipped, brute-forced, or whose result is trusted from the client

process.action: Map the full login sequence and identify the exact request that marks 2FA as satisfied
process.expected_observation: A specific response/parameter (e.g. mfa_verified=true) indicates second-factor completion

process.action: Attempt to access post-login resources directly after only completing step one (password), skipping the 2FA request entirely
process.expected_observation: Protected resource accessible without ever submitting a valid second factor

process.action: Test the second-factor code for brute-forceability (short numeric OTP, no lockout/rate limit)
process.expected_observation: Correct OTP found via exhaustive/high-volume guessing without being locked out

process.action: Test whether the 2FA verification result is trusted from a client-controllable parameter rather than re-checked server-side

impact: Complete bypass of the account's second authentication factor, negating its security benefit
Account takeover even when the victim has MFA enabled
remediation: Enforce second-factor completion as a required server-side session state, checked on every sensitive request
Rate-limit and lock out OTP attempts; use sufficiently long/random codes
Never trust a client-supplied flag as proof that verification occurred

title: FRAMESHIFTER: Security Implications of HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1 Conversion Anomalies

preconditions: A front-end proxy/load balancer and back-end server disagree on request boundary parsing (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding)

process.action: Identify the presence of a front-end/back-end architecture (CDN, reverse proxy, load balancer)
process.expected_observation: Distinct server signatures/headers suggest a multi-hop architecture

process.action: Send ambiguous requests with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers using known desync techniques (CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE)
process.expected_observation: Timing or response anomalies indicate the two servers parsed the request boundary differently

process.action: Confirm smuggling by injecting a full 'shadow' request in the body and observing its effect on the next unrelated request/response
process.expected_observation: A subsequent, unrelated request/response is contaminated by the smuggled request

process.action: Escalate to a targeted impact: cache poisoning, session hijacking of another user's request, or security control bypass
process.expected_observation: Attacker-controlled content is served to a victim, or a security control (e.g. auth check) is bypassed

impact: Hijacking of other users' requests/responses, including session token theft
Cache poisoning affecting all users of the shared cache
Bypass of front-end security controls (WAF, auth) that the back-end alone would not have allowed
remediation: Ensure front-end and back-end servers agree on request parsing (prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end, or normalize at the edge)
Reject ambiguous requests containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
Keep proxy/server software patched against known desync behaviors

title: How I Gained Access To A Finance Company’s Accounts (Session Hijacking)

preconditions: A weakness exists in an identity-related flow (password reset, email change, session handling, OAuth linking) that can be abused without knowing the victim's credentials

process.action: Map every identity-affecting flow: signup, login, password reset, email/phone change, social login linking
process.expected_observation: Full list of flows that can change or grant access to account control

process.action: Test each flow for weak or predictable tokens (short OTPs, sequential reset tokens, no rate limiting)
process.expected_observation: Token space is small enough to brute-force, or not invalidated after use

process.action: Test for host header / parameter injection in password reset emails that could leak the reset token to an attacker-controlled domain
process.expected_observation: Reset link is generated using an attacker-supplied host

process.action: Test race conditions or logic flaws in multi-step verification (e.g. completing OAuth linking before email ownership is verified)
process.expected_observation: Account control is granted despite incomplete verification

impact: Complete compromise of the victim's account and any data/permissions it holds
Downstream compromise of any service the account has SSO/linked access to
remediation: Use long, single-use, time-limited, cryptographically random tokens for all identity flows
Rate-limit and lock out after repeated failed verification attempts
Validate the Host header against an allow-list before using it to build links sent to users

title: A Developer’s Nightmare: Story of a simple IDOR and some poor fixes worth $1125

preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies

process.action: Map every endpoint that accepts an object identifier
process.expected_observation: List of endpoints with id-like parameters (order_id, user_id, file, uuid)

process.action: Record a baseline request/response as user A for an object A owns

title: How I Test For Web Cache Vulnerabilities + Tips And Tricks

preconditions: A shared cache stores responses keyed on a subset of the request that excludes an input the origin server's response actually varies on (an 'unkeyed input')

process.action: Identify cacheable responses and the cache key components (via cache-control/age headers and response timing)
process.expected_observation: Response is confirmed cacheable and shared across requests

process.action: Discover unkeyed inputs (headers/params that affect the response but are not part of the cache key)
process.expected_observation: A header (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) changes the response content without changing the cache key

process.action: Inject a malicious value into the unkeyed input (e.g. attacker domain into X-Forwarded-Host used to build a resource URL) and trigger caching of the poisoned response
process.expected_observation: Poisoned response is cached with attacker-controlled content

process.action: Verify a subsequent unauthenticated request retrieves the poisoned, cached response
process.expected_observation: Victim requests receive the attacker-controlled content directly from cache

impact: Mass client-side attack (XSS/malicious redirect) served to every visitor via the shared cache
Denial of service by poisoning the cache with error responses
remediation: Ensure the cache key includes every input that affects the response, or strip/normalize unkeyed inputs at the edge
Validate and canonicalize headers like Host/X-Forwarded-Host before using them to construct responses
Use short cache TTLs and cache-busting validation for sensitive/dynamic content

title: Hertzbleed Attack

scenario.summary: Cryptographic Issues writeup against Intel, Cloudflare, Microsoft.
preconditions: The application relies on encryption, hashing, or a TLS/certificate chain for confidentiality or integrity guarantees, using a weak algorithm, insufficient key length, predictable randomness, or improperly validated certificates

process.action: Identify where cryptography is used: password storage, token generation, data-at-rest encryption, TLS configuration, signed URLs/tokens
process.expected_observation: List of cryptographic usage points and their apparent algorithm/parameters

process.action: Fingerprint the algorithm/parameters in use (hash type, cipher suite, key length, TLS version) via response headers, token structure, or protocol handshake
process.expected_observation: A weak/deprecated algorithm identified (MD5, SHA1 for passwords, RC4, TLS 1.0, ECB mode, predictable PRNG)

process.action: For certificate validation, test whether the client (mobile app, backend service) properly validates the presented certificate chain, hostname, and expiry
process.expected_observation: A self-signed or mismatched certificate is silently accepted, enabling MITM interception

process.action: Attempt to exploit the weakness directly: crack weakly-hashed values offline, decrypt data using a known/derivable key, or predict a 'random' token from observed outputs
process.expected_observation: Plaintext recovered, or future token values predicted from the observed weakness

impact: Recovery of plaintext credentials/data protected only by weak cryptography
Man-in-the-middle interception of traffic when certificate validation is broken
Forgery of tokens/signed data when the underlying randomness or algorithm is predictable
remediation: Use current, vetted algorithms and parameters (e.g. bcrypt/argon2 for passwords, AES-GCM for encryption, TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites)
Enforce full certificate chain and hostname validation on every client, with no debug-mode bypass shipped to production
Use a cryptographically secure random number generator for any security-relevant randomness (tokens, IVs, session identifiers)

title: HDiff: A Semi-automatic Framework for Discovering Semantic Gap Attack in HTTP Implementations

preconditions: A front-end proxy/load balancer and back-end server disagree on request boundary parsing (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding)

process.action: Identify the presence of a front-end/back-end architecture (CDN, reverse proxy, load balancer)

process.action: Confirm smuggling by injecting a full 'shadow' request in the body and observing its effect on the next unrelated request/response

process.action: Escalate to a targeted impact: cache poisoning, session hijacking of another user's request, or security control bypass
process.expected_observation: Attacker-controlled content is served to a victim, or a security control (e.g. auth check) is bypassed

impact: Hijacking of other users' requests/responses, including session token theft
Cache poisoning affecting all users of the shared cache

remediation: Ensure front-end and back-end servers agree on request parsing (prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end, or normalize at the edge)
Reject ambiguous requests containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
Keep proxy/server software patched against known desync behaviors

title: The Story of a RCE on a Java Web Application

preconditions: Application deserializes untrusted data (cookies, cache objects, API payloads) using a language-native serializer capable of instantiating arbitrary objects

process.expected_observation: Base64/binary blob matches a known serialization format (Java, PHP, Python pickle, .NET)

process.action: Confirm the server actually deserializes the value by sending a malformed object and observing a deserialization-specific error
process.expected_observation: Stack trace or error references the deserializer class

process.action: Identify or generate a gadget chain appropriate to the target language/libraries
process.expected_observation: Known gadget chain available for the detected libraries in use

process.action: Craft and deliver a payload for a benign proof action (sleep, DNS callback) before attempting full RCE
process.expected_observation: Callback confirms code execution via deserialization

impact: Remote code execution on the server
Bypass of application logic by forging internal object state
remediation: Avoid deserializing untrusted data; prefer data formats without executable semantics (e.g. JSON with a strict schema)
If native serialization is required, use integrity-checked/signed payloads and restrict deserializable types (allow-list)
Keep serialization libraries patched against known gadget chains

title: How I found (and fixed) a vulnerability in Python

scenario.summary: Web Cache Poisoning writeup against Python.
preconditions: A shared cache stores responses keyed on a subset of the request that excludes an input the origin server's response actually varies on (an 'unkeyed input')

process.action: Identify cacheable responses and the cache key components (via cache-control/age headers and response timing)
process.expected_observation: Response is confirmed cacheable and shared across requests

process.action: Discover unkeyed inputs (headers/params that affect the response but are not part of the cache key)
process.expected_observation: A header (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) changes the response content without changing the cache key

process.action: Inject a malicious value into the unkeyed input (e.g. attacker domain into X-Forwarded-Host used to build a resource URL) and trigger caching of the poisoned response
process.expected_observation: Poisoned response is cached with attacker-controlled content

process.action: Verify a subsequent unauthenticated request retrieves the poisoned, cached response
process.expected_observation: Victim requests receive the attacker-controlled content directly from cache

impact: Mass client-side attack (XSS/malicious redirect) served to every visitor via the shared cache
Denial of service by poisoning the cache with error responses
remediation: Ensure the cache key includes every input that affects the response, or strip/normalize unkeyed inputs at the edge
Validate and canonicalize headers like Host/X-Forwarded-Host before using them to construct responses
Use short cache TTLs and cache-busting validation for sensitive/dynamic content

An input point that reaches a database query is reachable pre- or post-auth

process.action: Identify parameters that influence database-backed responses (search, filters, sort, IDs)
process.expected_observation: Parameter values affect returned data set

process.action: Send syntax-breaking probes (single quote, boolean true/false pairs) and diff responses
process.expected_observation: Error message, status code, or content length differs between true/false conditions

process.action: Confirm injection class (error-based, boolean-blind, time-based blind, UNION-based)
process.expected_observation: Consistent, controllable behavior change tied to injected logic

process.action: Enumerate database metadata (version, current user, schema) via the confirmed technique
process.expected_observation: Database name/version/table names extracted

process.action: Extract sensitive table contents or attempt privilege escalation (e.g. UNION into admin tables, stacked queries)
process.expected_observation: Sensitive data retrieved, confirming full impact

impact: Full database read/write, including credentials and PII
Authentication bypass via crafted login queries
In some configurations, OS command execution via database features (e.g. xp_cmdshell)
remediation: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements exclusively; never concatenate user input into SQL
Apply least-privilege database accounts per application function
Add a WAF as defense-in-depth, not as the primary control

title: Zero Click To Account Takeover

preconditions: A weakness exists in an identity-related flow (password reset, email change, session handling, OAuth linking) that can be abused without knowing the victim's credentials

process.action: Map every identity-affecting flow: signup, login, password reset, email/phone change, social login linking
process.expected_observation: Full list of flows that can change or grant access to account control

process.action: Test each flow for weak or predictable tokens (short OTPs, sequential reset tokens, no rate limiting)
process.expected_observation: Token space is small enough to brute-force, or not invalidated after use

process.action: Test for host header / parameter injection in password reset emails that could leak the reset token to an attacker-controlled domain
process.expected_observation: Reset link is generated using an attacker-supplied host

process.action: Test race conditions or logic flaws in multi-step verification (e.g. completing OAuth linking before email ownership is verified)
process.expected_observation: Account control is granted despite incomplete verification

impact: Complete compromise of the victim's account and any data/permissions it holds
Downstream compromise of any service the account has SSO/linked access to
remediation: Use long, single-use, time-limited, cryptographically random tokens for all identity flows
Rate-limit and lock out after repeated failed verification attempts
Validate the Host header against an allow-list before using it to build links sent to users

scenario.summary: Path Traversal writeup against Grafana Labs.
preconditions: A parameter controls a filename/path that is used in a filesystem read/include operation without normalization

process.action: Identify the presence of a front-end/back-end architecture (CDN, reverse proxy, load balancer)
process.expected_observation: Distinct server signatures/headers suggest a multi-hop architecture

process.action: Send ambiguous requests with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers using known desync techniques (CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE)
process.expected_observation: Timing or response anomalies indicate the two servers parsed the request boundary differently

process.action: Confirm smuggling by injecting a full 'shadow' request in the body and observing its effect on the next unrelated request/response
process.expected_observation: A subsequent, unrelated request/response is contaminated by the smuggled request

process.action: Escalate to a targeted impact: cache poisoning, session hijacking of another user's request, or security control bypass
process.expected_observation: Attacker-controlled content is served to a victim, or a security control (e.g. auth check) is bypassed

impact: Hijacking of other users' requests/responses, including session token theft
Cache poisoning affecting all users of the shared cache
Bypass of front-end security controls (WAF, auth) that the back-end alone would not have allowed
remediation: Ensure front-end and back-end servers agree on request parsing (prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end, or normalize at the edge)
Reject ambiguous requests containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
Keep proxy/server software patched against known desync behaviors

preconditions: A state-changing endpoint relies solely on session cookies for authentication
No anti-CSRF token, SameSite cookie protection, or origin validation is enforced

process.action: Identify state-changing endpoints (password change, email change, fund transfer)
process.expected_observation: List of sensitive POST/PUT/DELETE endpoints

process.action: Check for anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookie attributes, and Origin/Referer validation

process.action: Build a proof-of-concept auto-submitting HTML form/fetch that replays the request cross-origin
process.expected_observation: Request succeeds when submitted from a foreign origin while the victim's session cookie is attached

process.action: Validate the PoC against a real authenticated session in a browser (not just a proxy replay)
process.expected_observation: State change occurs on the victim's account after visiting the malicious page

remediation: Implement per-session, per-request anti-CSRF tokens validated server-side
Set cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict where compatible with the application's flows
Validate Origin/Referer headers on state-changing requests as defense-in-depth

process.expected_observation: Canary characters are not encoded when rendered

process.action: Replace canary with an executing payload appropriate to the render context
process.expected_observation: JavaScript executes for any user who views the content

process.action: Assess blast radius (does it fire for admins/all users or a limited audience)

remediation: Sanitize on input using an allow-list HTML sanitizer for rich-text fields
Encode on output regardless of input sanitization (defense in depth)
Apply CSP and isolate untrusted rendered content (e.g. sandboxed iframes) where rich content is required

title: $600 for IDOR (File or Folder Download)

preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies

preconditions: A workflow assumes steps happen in a fixed order or trusts client-supplied values (price, quantity, state) that should be server-authoritative

title: Ping'ing XMLSec

scenario.summary: XML External Entity (XXE) Injection writeup against Ping, Netflix, Paypal.
preconditions: The application parses XML input with an XML parser that has external entity resolution enabled

process.action: Identify endpoints that accept XML directly or indirectly (SOAP, file uploads like DOCX/SVG, SAML)
process.expected_observation: XML-consuming endpoints identified

process.action: Submit a DOCTYPE with a benign external entity referencing an internal file
process.expected_observation: File content is reflected in the response, or an out-of-band callback fires

process.expected_observation: Requested file content is exfiltrated via the OOB channel

process.action: Attempt SSRF via XXE (fetching internal URLs/cloud metadata through the XML parser)

SSRF pivot into internal network resources

title: "A tale of making internet pollution free" - Exploiting Client-Side Prototype Pollution in the wild

scenario.summary: Prototype Pollution writeup against Apple, Atlassian, Mozilla, HubSpot, Segment Analytics.
preconditions: JavaScript code merges/clones user-controlled objects using a recursive merge that does not block __proto__/constructor.prototype keys

process.action: Identify client- or server-side JS code paths that merge user input into an object (deep merge, clone, JSON parse into config)
process.expected_observation: Recursive merge/assign function reachable with attacker-controlled keys

process.action: Submit a payload with a __proto__ or constructor.prototype key to attempt polluting Object.prototype
process.expected_observation: A new property appears on all objects (e.g. {}.polluted === 'yes')

process.action: Identify a gadget that consumes the polluted property in a security-sensitive way (e.g. an isAdmin default, template rendering flag)
process.expected_observation: Application behavior changes based on the polluted global property

process.action: Chain the pollution with the identified gadget to achieve a concrete impact (privilege escalation, XSS, DoS)
process.expected_observation: Concrete security impact (e.g. unauthorized admin UI rendered) confirmed

impact: Denial of service via crashing application logic
Privilege escalation or XSS when a polluted property is consumed by a security-relevant gadget
remediation: Use Object.create(null) or Map for user-controlled key/value storage instead of plain objects
Use merge/clone libraries that explicitly block __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys
Freeze Object.prototype in sensitive contexts where feasible

title: Zero-Day: Hijacking iCloud Credentials with Apple Airtags (Stored XSS)

scenario.summary: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) writeup against Apple.
preconditions: Application persists user-supplied content (comments, profile fields, file metadata) and later renders it to other users
Stored content is not sanitized/encoded on output

process.action: Identify fields whose stored value is later rendered to other users (not just the submitter)
process.expected_observation: Stored value reappears on a different page/view/account

process.action: Submit a canary payload into the field and confirm storage
process.expected_observation: Canary is saved without modification

process.action: Trigger the rendering path as a victim/other user session
process.expected_observation: Canary characters are not encoded when rendered

process.action: Replace canary with an executing payload appropriate to the render context
process.expected_observation: JavaScript executes for any user who views the content

process.action: Assess blast radius (does it fire for admins/all users or a limited audience)
process.expected_observation: Determine if privileged users are affected, raising severity

impact: Persistent compromise of every user who views the affected content, including administrators
Mass session/token theft or worm-like propagation
Full account takeover at scale
remediation: Sanitize on input using an allow-list HTML sanitizer for rich-text fields
Encode on output regardless of input sanitization (defense in depth)
Apply CSP and isolate untrusted rendered content (e.g. sandboxed iframes) where rich content is required

title: DeepSurface Security Advisory: LPE in Firefox on Windows

scenario.summary: Broken Access Control / Privilege Escalation writeup against Mozilla.
preconditions: Role/permission checks are missing or misapplied on at least one code path
Multiple privilege levels exist (e.g. user vs admin, tenant A vs tenant B)

process.action: Enumerate role-restricted functionality from the UI/API docs for a higher-privileged role
process.expected_observation: List of admin/privileged-only endpoints

process.action: Attempt to access each privileged endpoint using a low-privilege account's session
process.expected_observation: Privileged endpoint responds successfully despite low-privilege session

process.action: Test cross-tenant/cross-org access using valid low-privilege credentials against another tenant's resources
process.expected_observation: Cross-tenant data is returned

process.action: Attempt role-elevation via mass assignment (submitting an unexpected role/permission field in a profile update)
process.expected_observation: Server accepts and applies the unauthorized field, elevating privileges

impact: Unauthorized access to administrative functionality or another tenant's data
Full account/organization compromise depending on the privilege gained
remediation: Centralize authorization logic (policy engine/middleware) rather than per-endpoint ad hoc checks
Deny by default; explicitly allow-list which roles can reach which endpoints
Apply tenant-scoping at the data-access layer, not just in application logic

title: Bypass of biometrics & password security functionality for Android

preconditions: An authentication check can be skipped or forged via parameter manipulation, alternate endpoint, or logic flaw

process.action: Map the full authentication flow, including alternate/legacy endpoints (mobile API, password reset, SSO)
process.expected_observation: Multiple entry points to authenticated state identified

process.action: Test for direct object/endpoint access without a valid session (forced browsing)
process.expected_observation: Protected resource accessible without authentication

process.action: Test parameter-based bypass (role=admin, isAdmin=true, X-Original-URL headers, JWT alg=none)
process.expected_observation: Server trusts a client-supplied privilege claim

process.action: Test multi-step flow logic (e.g. skipping a step in MFA/password reset by calling a later-stage endpoint directly)
process.expected_observation: Later-stage endpoint succeeds without completing earlier required steps

impact: Unauthorized access to protected functionality or data
Full account takeover if the bypass grants another user's session or privileges
remediation: Enforce authentication and authorization checks server-side on every request, independent of client-supplied state
Ensure multi-step flows validate that prior steps were actually completed (server-side state, not client-trusted flags)
Use signed, algorithm-pinned tokens (reject 'alg: none' and algorithm confusion in JWTs)

title: Improper phone number validation to account takeover

preconditions: A weakness exists in an identity-related flow (password reset, email change, session handling, OAuth linking) that can be abused without knowing the victim's credentials

process.action: Map every identity-affecting flow: signup, login, password reset, email/phone change, social login linking
process.expected_observation: Full list of flows that can change or grant access to account control

process.action: Test each flow for weak or predictable tokens (short OTPs, sequential reset tokens, no rate limiting)
process.expected_observation: Token space is small enough to brute-force, or not invalidated after use

process.action: Test for host header / parameter injection in password reset emails that could leak the reset token to an attacker-controlled domain
process.expected_observation: Reset link is generated using an attacker-supplied host

process.action: Test race conditions or logic flaws in multi-step verification (e.g. completing OAuth linking before email ownership is verified)
process.expected_observation: Account control is granted despite incomplete verification

impact: Complete compromise of the victim's account and any data/permissions it holds
Downstream compromise of any service the account has SSO/linked access to
remediation: Use long, single-use, time-limited, cryptographically random tokens for all identity flows
Rate-limit and lock out after repeated failed verification attempts
Validate the Host header against an allow-list before using it to build links sent to users

title: Attack Surface Analysis - Part 3 - Resurrected Code Execution

preconditions: An input reaches a dangerous sink that evaluates or executes it (template engine, deserializer, shell command, file include)

process.action: Identify features that process user-supplied files, templates, or serialized data server-side
process.expected_observation: Upload/import/render features that touch interpreters or parsers

process.action: Probe for the specific sink class (SSTI, deserialization, command injection, unsafe file include)
process.expected_observation: Error messages or timing differences reveal the underlying engine/language

process.action: Send a benign proof payload (e.g. arithmetic in a template, sleep command) to confirm execution without causing damage
process.expected_observation: Evaluated result (e.g. computed number, delayed response) confirms code execution

process.action: Escalate to a controlled, reversible action (e.g. read a known file, DNS callback) to fully confirm RCE
process.expected_observation: Out-of-band callback received or file content returned, proving arbitrary execution

impact: Full compromise of the application server and any data it can access
Lateral movement into internal network and other services
Complete loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability for the affected system
remediation: Never pass user input into eval/exec/template-render/deserialization functions
Sandbox or disable dangerous interpreter features when user-influenced execution is unavoidable
Apply least-privilege execution contexts (containers, restricted service accounts) to limit blast radius

title: $8,000 Bug Bounty Highlight: XSS to RCE in the Opera Browser

scenario.summary: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) writeup against Opera.
preconditions: User-controlled input (query params, form fields, headers) is reflected in the HTML response
No or insufficient output encoding/CSP is applied to the reflected context

process.action: Identify all input points that are echoed back in the response
process.expected_observation: Input value appears unmodified in the HTML/JS/attribute context

process.action: Determine the reflection context (HTML body, attribute, JS string, URL)
process.expected_observation: Context dictates which payload shape will execute

process.action: Send a canary payload to confirm reflection without encoding
process.expected_observation: Special characters like < > " ' pass through unescaped

process.action: Craft a context-appropriate payload that breaks out and executes JavaScript
process.expected_observation: JavaScript executes in the victim's browser origin (e.g. alert/document.cookie access)

process.action: Verify real-world exploitability by delivering the payload via a crafted link and checking for CSP/WAF bypass needs
process.expected_observation: Payload fires when a victim visits the crafted URL

impact: Session hijacking via cookie/token theft
Actions performed on behalf of the victim (CSRF-like impact)
Credential phishing or malicious redirect within a trusted origin
remediation: Context-aware output encoding for every reflection point (HTML, attribute, JS, URL encoding as appropriate)
Deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy with no unsafe-inline
Use framework-level auto-escaping templates instead of manual string concatenation

title: A fever Worth 750$- [Accessing Private Projects ]

scenario.summary: Sensitive Information Disclosure writeup against Mozilla.
preconditions: An endpoint, error message, or artifact exposes data beyond what the requesting party should be entitled to see

process.action: Review responses (including error pages, verbose stack traces, API responses) for unintended data
process.expected_observation: Stack traces, internal paths, or extra object fields present in responses

process.action: Check for over-fetching in API responses (fields returned but not rendered by the client)
process.expected_observation: API response includes sensitive fields not shown in the UI (e.g. hashed password, internal notes)

process.action: Check for exposed artifacts (backup files, .git directories, debug endpoints, cloud storage buckets)
process.expected_observation: Sensitive file or exposed storage bucket accessible without authentication

process.action: Assess sensitivity and reachability of the exposed data to determine severity
process.expected_observation: Data classified (PII, credentials, internal source) and access path confirmed unauthenticated/low-privilege

impact: Exposure of PII, credentials, or internal implementation details aiding further attacks
Direct regulatory/compliance impact if regulated data (health, financial) is exposed
remediation: Return only the minimum fields required by the client (explicit response DTOs, not raw model serialization)
Disable verbose error/debug output in production
Regularly audit cloud storage and repository exposure for accidental public access

title: Cookie Stealing via Clickjacking using Burp collaborator

preconditions: A sensitive action page can be rendered inside an iframe with no framing protection (X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors)

process.action: Check response headers of sensitive pages for X-Frame-Options and CSP frame-ancestors directives
process.expected_observation: No framing-protection header present, or set to a permissive value

process.action: Build a PoC page that iframes the target page and overlays deceptive UI elements
process.expected_observation: Target page renders inside the attacker's iframe

process.action: Align invisible/transparent target UI elements under decoy content to trick a click
process.expected_observation: A click on the decoy actually triggers the sensitive action on the framed page

process.action: Validate the sensitive action (e.g. enabling a setting, submitting a form) actually executes when a test click lands
process.expected_observation: Victim's click results in the unintended sensitive action being performed

impact: Victim tricked into performing unintended state-changing actions on an authenticated session
Combined with other flaws, can lead to account settings changes or unauthorized authorizations
remediation: Set X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN, and/or CSP frame-ancestors, on all sensitive pages
Add frame-busting JavaScript as defense-in-depth for legacy browser support

title: RCE in Citrix ShareFile Storage Zones Controller (CVE-2021-22941) – A Walk-Through

scenario.summary: Path Traversal writeup against Citrix Systems.
preconditions: A parameter controls a filename/path that is used in a filesystem read/include operation without normalization

process.action: Identify parameters that reference filenames or paths (download, template, avatar, report)
process.expected_observation: Parameter value maps to a served file

process.action: Inject traversal sequences (../, encoded variants, null bytes) targeting a known OS file
process.expected_observation: Known file content (e.g. /etc/passwd, win.ini) is returned

process.action: Bypass filtering (double encoding, path normalization quirks, absolute paths) if naive traversal is blocked
process.expected_observation: Traversal succeeds despite basic sanitization

process.action: Escalate to reading application source/config files to extract secrets, or to local file inclusion for code execution if the language supports it
process.expected_observation: Sensitive config/secrets retrieved, or included file executes as code

impact: Disclosure of sensitive files (source code, credentials, configuration)
In LFI-capable stacks, potential remote code execution via log/session poisoning
remediation: Resolve and validate the final canonical path against an allow-listed base directory before any file operation
Avoid passing user input directly into filesystem APIs; use indirect identifiers mapped server-side
Run the application with filesystem permissions scoped to only what it needs

title: Breaking Application’s Logic to DOS Attack

preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies
Two accounts of the same privilege level are available for differential testing
Access control checks are applied inconsistently across endpoints

process.action: Map every endpoint that accepts an object identifier
process.expected_observation: List of endpoints with id-like parameters (order_id, user_id, file, uuid)

process.action: Record a baseline request/response as user A for an object A owns
process.expected_observation: 200 response containing user A's own object data

process.action: Replay the same request using user B's session/token but referencing object A's identifier
process.expected_observation: If access control is broken, the response returns user A's object data to user B

process.action: Enumerate adjacent identifiers (sequential IDs, predictable UUIDs) to confirm the issue is systemic, not a one-off
process.expected_observation: Multiple unrelated objects accessible across the ID space

process.action: Test write/delete operations (not just read) on the same identifier pattern
process.expected_observation: Unauthorized modification or deletion succeeds

impact: Unauthorized read access to other users' private data
Unauthorized modification or deletion of other users' resources
Potential account takeover if the exposed object includes credentials or session tokens
remediation: Enforce server-side ownership/authorization checks on every object access, not just at the UI layer
Use indirect, non-guessable references (per-user mapping tokens) instead of raw sequential IDs where feasible
Add automated authorization tests to CI that assert cross-account access is denied

No anti-CSRF token, SameSite cookie protection, or origin validation is enforced

process.action: Identify state-changing endpoints (password change, email change, fund transfer)
process.expected_observation: List of sensitive POST/PUT/DELETE endpoints

process.action: Check for anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookie attributes, and Origin/Referer validation
process.expected_observation: No token required, or token not validated server-side; cookie is SameSite=None or unset

process.action: Build a proof-of-concept auto-submitting HTML form/fetch that replays the request cross-origin
process.expected_observation: Request succeeds when submitted from a foreign origin while the victim's session cookie is attached

process.action: Validate the PoC against a real authenticated session in a browser (not just a proxy replay)
process.expected_observation: State change occurs on the victim's account after visiting the malicious page

impact: Unauthorized state changes performed as the victim (password/email change, fund transfer, privilege grant)
Chained with XSS or open redirect, can lead to full account takeover
remediation: Implement per-session, per-request anti-CSRF tokens validated server-side
Set cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict where compatible with the application's flows
Validate Origin/Referer headers on state-changing requests as defense-in-depth

title: Some ways to find more IDOR

preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies
Two accounts of the same privilege level are available for differential testing
Access control checks are applied inconsistently across endpoints

process.action: Map every endpoint that accepts an object identifier
process.expected_observation: List of endpoints with id-like parameters (order_id, user_id, file, uuid)

process.action: Record a baseline request/response as user A for an object A owns
process.expected_observation: 200 response containing user A's own object data

process.action: Replay the same request using user B's session/token but referencing object A's identifier
process.expected_observation: If access control is broken, the response returns user A's object data to user B

process.action: Enumerate adjacent identifiers (sequential IDs, predictable UUIDs) to confirm the issue is systemic, not a one-off
process.expected_observation: Multiple unrelated objects accessible across the ID space

process.action: Test write/delete operations (not just read) on the same identifier pattern
process.expected_observation: Unauthorized modification or deletion succeeds

impact: Unauthorized read access to other users' private data
Unauthorized modification or deletion of other users' resources
Potential account takeover if the exposed object includes credentials or session tokens
remediation: Enforce server-side ownership/authorization checks on every object access, not just at the UI layer
Use indirect, non-guessable references (per-user mapping tokens) instead of raw sequential IDs where feasible
Add automated authorization tests to CI that assert cross-account access is denied

title: Microsoft Store free purschase vulnerabilites

scenario.summary: Business Logic Flaw writeup against Microsoft.
preconditions: A workflow assumes steps happen in a fixed order or trusts client-supplied values (price, quantity, state) that should be server-authoritative

process.action: Map the full multi-step workflow (cart -> discount -> payment -> confirmation) and note every client-supplied value
process.expected_observation: List of values the client sends that influence the final outcome (price, quantity, currency, state transitions)

process.action: Tamper with server-authoritative-seeming values (price, discount code reuse, negative quantities)
process.expected_observation: Server accepts an inconsistent or attacker-favorable value

process.action: Attempt to skip or reorder workflow steps by calling later-stage endpoints directly
process.expected_observation: Later step succeeds without the required prior step (e.g. payment confirmed without payment)

process.action: Test boundary and negative values (zero/negative price, quantity overflow) for unexpected acceptance
process.expected_observation: Application processes an invalid business value as if valid

impact: Financial loss (free/discounted purchases, negative-price refund abuse)
Workflow bypass leading to unauthorized end states (e.g. order marked shipped without payment)
remediation: Recompute and validate all business-critical values server-side; never trust client-supplied price/quantity/state
Enforce workflow state machines server-side so steps cannot be skipped or reordered
Add server-side sanity bounds on numeric business values

title: Generate online votes using Race Condition Vulnerability in Woobox Web Application (Write Up)

preconditions: A multi-step operation (balance check then debit, coupon redemption, limited-use action) is not protected by atomic/locking guarantees

process.action: Identify operations with a check-then-act pattern and a limited resource (balance, single-use coupon, invite quota)
process.expected_observation: Candidate endpoint where a value is checked, then consumed, in separate steps

process.action: Send a baseline single request and record the resulting state change
process.expected_observation: One unit of the resource is consumed per request under normal conditions

process.action: Send many identical requests concurrently to win the race window between check and act
process.expected_observation: Multiple requests succeed against a resource meant to be single-use

process.action: Verify the resulting inconsistent state (e.g. balance went negative, coupon used multiple times)
process.expected_observation: Final state shows more consumption than should have been possible

impact: Financial loss via double-spending, multiple coupon redemption, or balance manipulation
Bypass of rate/quota limits meant to prevent abuse
remediation: Use database-level atomic operations or row locking for check-then-act sequences
Apply idempotency keys to prevent duplicate processing of the same logical request
Add application-level distributed locks around single-use resource consumption

title: Stored XSS via Invite leading to Mass Account Takeover at Opera.

scenario.summary: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) writeup against Opera.
preconditions: Application persists user-supplied content (comments, profile fields, file metadata) and later renders it to other users
Stored content is not sanitized/encoded on output

process.action: Identify fields whose stored value is later rendered to other users (not just the submitter)
process.expected_observation: Stored value reappears on a different page/view/account

process.action: Submit a canary payload into the field and confirm storage
process.expected_observation: Canary is saved without modification

process.action: Trigger the rendering path as a victim/other user session
process.expected_observation: Canary characters are not encoded when rendered

process.action: Replace canary with an executing payload appropriate to the render context
process.expected_observation: JavaScript executes for any user who views the content

process.action: Assess blast radius (does it fire for admins/all users or a limited audience)
process.expected_observation: Determine if privileged users are affected, raising severity

impact: Persistent compromise of every user who views the affected content, including administrators
Mass session/token theft or worm-like propagation
Full account takeover at scale
remediation: Sanitize on input using an allow-list HTML sanitizer for rich-text fields

Apply CSP and isolate untrusted rendered content (e.g. sandboxed iframes) where rich content is required

preconditions: A weakness exists in an identity-related flow (password reset, email change, session handling, OAuth linking) that can be abused without knowing the victim's credentials

process.expected_observation: Full list of flows that can change or grant access to account control

process.action: Test each flow for weak or predictable tokens (short OTPs, sequential reset tokens, no rate limiting)

process.action: Identify the presence of a front-end/back-end architecture (CDN, reverse proxy, load balancer)
process.expected_observation: Distinct server signatures/headers suggest a multi-hop architecture

process.action: Send ambiguous requests with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers using known desync techniques (CL.TE, TE.CL, TE.TE)
process.expected_observation: Timing or response anomalies indicate the two servers parsed the request boundary differently

process.action: Confirm smuggling by injecting a full 'shadow' request in the body and observing its effect on the next unrelated request/response
process.expected_observation: A subsequent, unrelated request/response is contaminated by the smuggled request

process.action: Escalate to a targeted impact: cache poisoning, session hijacking of another user's request, or security control bypass
process.expected_observation: Attacker-controlled content is served to a victim, or a security control (e.g. auth check) is bypassed

impact: Hijacking of other users' requests/responses, including session token theft
Cache poisoning affecting all users of the shared cache
Bypass of front-end security controls (WAF, auth) that the back-end alone would not have allowed
remediation: Ensure front-end and back-end servers agree on request parsing (prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end, or normalize at the edge)
Reject ambiguous requests containing both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding
Keep proxy/server software patched against known desync behaviors

preconditions: A workflow assumes steps happen in a fixed order or trusts client-supplied values (price, quantity, state) that should be server-authoritative

process.action: Map the full multi-step workflow (cart -> discount -> payment -> confirmation) and note every client-supplied value

process.action: Tamper with server-authoritative-seeming values (price, discount code reuse, negative quantities)

process.action: Attempt to skip or reorder workflow steps by calling later-stage endpoints directly
process.expected_observation: Later step succeeds without the required prior step (e.g. payment confirmed without payment)

process.action: Test boundary and negative values (zero/negative price, quantity overflow) for unexpected acceptance

Add server-side sanity bounds on numeric business values

title: Attacks On GCM With Repeated Nonces

preconditions: The application relies on encryption, hashing, or a TLS/certificate chain for confidentiality or integrity guarantees, using a weak algorithm, insufficient key length, predictable randomness, or improperly validated certificates

process.action: Identify where cryptography is used: password storage, token generation, data-at-rest encryption, TLS configuration, signed URLs/tokens
process.expected_observation: List of cryptographic usage points and their apparent algorithm/parameters

process.action: Fingerprint the algorithm/parameters in use (hash type, cipher suite, key length, TLS version) via response headers, token structure, or protocol handshake
process.expected_observation: A weak/deprecated algorithm identified (MD5, SHA1 for passwords, RC4, TLS 1.0, ECB mode, predictable PRNG)

process.action: For certificate validation, test whether the client (mobile app, backend service) properly validates the presented certificate chain, hostname, and expiry
process.expected_observation: A self-signed or mismatched certificate is silently accepted, enabling MITM interception

process.action: Attempt to exploit the weakness directly: crack weakly-hashed values offline, decrypt data using a known/derivable key, or predict a 'random' token from observed outputs
process.expected_observation: Plaintext recovered, or future token values predicted from the observed weakness

impact: Recovery of plaintext credentials/data protected only by weak cryptography
Man-in-the-middle interception of traffic when certificate validation is broken
Forgery of tokens/signed data when the underlying randomness or algorithm is predictable
remediation: Use current, vetted algorithms and parameters (e.g. bcrypt/argon2 for passwords, AES-GCM for encryption, TLS 1.2+ with strong cipher suites)
Enforce full certificate chain and hostname validation on every client, with no debug-mode bypass shipped to production
Use a cryptographically secure random number generator for any security-relevant randomness (tokens, IVs, session identifiers)
